lead: LALR is a middle ground between SLR and canonical LR(1). It keeps the small LR(0)-sized automaton but adds lookahead terminals to reductions. The trick is to merge LR(1) states that have the same core, then union their lookaheads. The result is often called LALR(1), for LookAhead LR. Parser generators such as YACC use it because it is compact and handles most programming-language grammars. The cost is risk: merging can create a reduce/reduce conflict that canonical LR(1) would not have.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.4 on canonical LR(1) items and states, plus the LR(0) automaton from Chapter 3.2.

sections.h3: Core of a state and the merge

blocks.text: An LR(1) item is [A → α . β, a]. A is the left-hand side; α and β are strings of grammar symbols; the dot shows how far parsing has moved; a is one lookahead symbol: a terminal or the special end-of-input marker $. The core of an LR(1) state is the set of items with the lookahead removed: {[A → α . β]}. Two states can have the same core and different lookaheads.
core(I) = { [A → α . β] | [A → α . β, a] ∈ I for some a }
blocks.where: I is an LR(1) state; A → αβ is a production; a is a lookahead symbol (a terminal or $).

blocks.text: LALR takes every group of LR(1) states with one core and replaces the group by one state. For each item, the new lookahead set is the union of the lookaheads from all states in the group. This is why LALR has LR(0)-size state counts but uses more precise lookaheads than SLR.

items: Build the canonical LR(1) states using Chapter 3.4.
Group states that have the same core.
Keep one state per group; the core does not change.
For each item, union the lookaheads from all states in the group.
Rebuild reduce actions from the unioned lookaheads and check for conflicts.

blocks.text: Merging can combine two reductions that were safe in separate states. Consider S → a A d | b B d | a B e | b A e, A → c, B → c. In the canonical LR(1) state reached after a and c, the items are A → c., d and B → c., e. On d only A reduces; on e only B reduces. No conflict.
In the canonical LR(1) state reached after b and c, the items are B → c., d and A → c., e. Again there is no conflict. Both states have the same core, {A → c., B → c.}, so LALR merges them.

The merged state has A → c., d/e and B → c., d/e. On d both A → c. and B → c. are possible reductions. On e both are also possible. That is a reduce/reduce conflict. This grammar is LR(1) but not LALR(1). Merging states with the same core does not create new shift/reduce conflicts here; it can create reduce/reduce conflicts.

sections.h3: Size and place in the LR family

blocks.text: For the grammar above, including the augmented start state, canonical LR(1) has 14 states. LR(0), SLR and LALR each have 13 states. LALR has the same number of states as LR(0) because merging by core exactly undoes the lookahead split. Some syllabi call this method LookAhead LR or LALR(1).

SLR uses FOLLOW sets, while LALR uses item lookaheads produced by merging. Canonical LR(1) is stronger. Its table can be larger because it may keep separate states with the same core; LALR has no more states than canonical LR(1). LALR is the usual choice when table size matters and the grammar is almost LR(1). Parser generators report the remaining conflicts, as covered in Chapter 3.6.

spec.aria: Two LR(1) states with items A → c. and B → c. carrying different lookaheads merge into one LALR state with lookaheads d/e, whose d and e entries each hold two reductions.

examples.question: Grammar: S → a A d | b B d | a B e | b A e, A → c, B → c. Build the canonical LR(1) states reached on c from the states after a and after b. Merge them into one LALR state. State the number of items in each LR(1) state, the number of reduce entries after merging, and the number of reduce/reduce conflict cells. Show the conflict.
steps: After a: items S → a . A d, $ and S → a . B e, $. Closure adds A → . c, d and B → . c, e.
Goto on c gives state I5: A → c., d and B → c., e. It has 2 items. On d only A reduces; on e only B reduces. No conflict.
After b: items S → b . B d, $ and S → b . A e, $. Closure adds B → . c, d and A → . c, e.
Goto on c gives state I8: B → c., d and A → c., e. It has 2 items. On d only B reduces; on e only A reduces. No conflict.
The core of I5 is {A → c., B → c.}. The core of I8 is {A → c., B → c.}. The cores are equal, so LALR merges I5 and I8.
The merged LALR state I58 has A → c., d/e and B → c., d/e. Each item has lookahead set {d, e}.
Reduce entries in I58: A on d, A on e, B on d, B on e. That is 4 entries.
On d, both A → c. and B → c. reduce. On e, both reduce. That is 2 reduce/reduce conflict cells.
examples.answer: Each LR(1) state has 2 items; the merged LALR state has 4 reduce entries and 2 reduce/reduce conflict cells, on d and e.

traps: LALR has LR(0)-size state counts, not canonical LR(1)-size counts. The lookaheads are more precise than SLR but the state count is not larger.
Merging unions lookaheads. Do not intersect lookaheads and do not keep only one state's lookahead.
New conflicts caused by merging are reduce/reduce, not new shift/reduce. A shift action depends on the core, which is identical in the merged states.
A grammar can be LR(1) and not LALR(1). The standard example is S → a A d | b B d | a B e | b A e, A → c, B → c.
SLR uses FOLLOW sets, LALR uses item lookaheads from merged LR(1) states. Do not replace an LALR lookahead with FOLLOW.

quiz.q: What does LALR stand for, and how many lookahead symbols does LALR(1) use?
quiz.a: LookAhead LR. LALR(1) uses one lookahead symbol: a terminal or the special end marker $.

quiz.q: Why does LALR merge LR(1) states with the same core?
quiz.a: To reduce the number of states to the LR(0) count while keeping lookahead information on reductions. This gives a smaller table than canonical LR(1).

quiz.q: In the worked example, list the lookaheads on A → c. in the merged state I58.
quiz.a: The lookaheads are d and e, written A → c., d/e. They come from the union of A → c., d and A → c., e.

quiz.q: Explain why the merged state I58 has a reduce/reduce conflict on d and e.
quiz.a: On d, both A → c. and B → c. are possible reductions. On e, both are also possible. The canonical states separated these by lookahead; the union puts both reductions under both lookaheads.

quiz.q: How many reduce entries does the merged state have in the worked example?
quiz.a: Four: A on d, A on e, B on d, B on e.

quiz.q: Can merging two LR(1) states with the same core create a new shift/reduce conflict? Give a reason.
quiz.a: No new shift/reduce conflict. The core fixes the shift and goto actions. If a reduce lookahead is added by union, the same shift already existed in a state with that core if it creates a shift/reduce conflict. Merging can add reduce/reduce conflicts.

quiz.q: How does the number of LALR states compare with LR(0) states and canonical LR(1) states?
quiz.a: LALR has the same number of states as LR(0). It has no more states than canonical LR(1); it is strictly smaller only when canonical LR(1) has separate states with the same core.

beyond: Not for the exam. LALR is the default in many parser generators because the tables are small and conflicts are rare. Some tools offer canonical LR(1) or IELR when a grammar is LR(1) but not LALR(1). Search terms: LALR merging, IELR, parser generator conflict report, grammar refactoring.
